pages.title: About
pages.content:
About

Neiro Music is a private music school for children and adult beginners, founded in 2011 by pianist Ilse Marchetti. It stands at Lindenhof 14, 9000 Ghent, Belgium, in a converted print works with two floors.

Meet the teachers

Philosophy

A school that began with one room

Six teaching rooms sit alongside the 60-seat Long Room, which is kept for pupil recitals. There are 240 pupils and eight teachers.

Lessons run Monday to Friday from 14:00 to 21:30 and Saturday from 09:00 to 18:00. The office answers the phone Monday to Friday from 13:00 to 18:00.

Ilse still teaches piano, and the same rooms that held the first pupils still set the scale of the work: one teacher, one pupil, one instrument, enough quiet to hear the next note.

About

2011

The first room

One teacher, one pupil, one instrument

Ilse Marchetti, pianist, opened Neiro Music in 2011 in a converted print works at Lindenhof 14. The first pupils had piano lessons in a single room, and that room still sets the scale of the work: enough quiet to hear the next note.

Visit the school

About

2016

The Long Room

Sixty chairs and a grand piano

Since 2016 the 60-seat Long Room has held the school's recitals, one in December and one in June. It is kept for pupil recitals and is not used for ordinary lessons.

Recitals and ensembles

About

Today

Eight teachers

240 pupils, thirty teaching weeks

There are 240 pupils and eight teachers across six teaching rooms. The year runs thirty weeks from September to June, and children begin piano or violin from five. Adults begin at any age.

A week at Neiro

pages.title: Lessons & Instruments
pages.content:
Instruments

Five instruments, taught one to one

Piano is taught from the age of five, and adults may begin at any age. A weekly lesson is 30, 45 or 60 minutes.

Piano, violin, cello, voice and guitar are all taught one to one in six teaching rooms. Prices are in EUR.

Fees and enrolment

Piano

From five, and adults at any age

Piano is taught from the age of five, and adults may begin at any age. A weekly lesson is 30, 45 or 60 minutes. For children, a 30-minute weekly lesson is €290 per term, and that term is ten lessons. Adult beginners take a 45-minute weekly lesson at €450 per term.

Violin is taught from the age of five by Léa Fournier, and Jonas Weber teaches cello. Strings lessons sit in the strings hour at 16:45. Children's strings are €290 per term at 30 minutes weekly, or €420 at 45 minutes.

Priya Raman teaches the adult piano class; Ilse Marchetti teaches piano as founder of the school. Adult beginners are in the rooms from 19:15.

pages.title: Teachers
pages.content:
Teachers

Eight teachers work at Neiro Music. Ilse Marchetti, pianist and founder, has taught piano here since she opened the school in 2011.

Fees and enrolment

Teachers

Eight teachers, one office

Tomás Rivera teaches guitar. Sofie De Smet runs the office and is not one of the eight teachers.

Between them they cover the instruments on the timetable: piano, violin, cello, voice and guitar, plus the theory table and the Friday ensemble. The Long Room, with its sixty seats, is used when the school gathers for the December and June recitals.

pages.title: Fees & Enrolment
pages.content:
Fees

Term fees in EUR

Fees are charged in EUR. What the term fee covers is the weekly lesson or group named in that line, across the teaching year of thirty weeks from September to June.

Trial lesson, 30 min

One meeting with a teacher before a pupil enrols.

€0

Children's piano or strings, 30 min weekly, per term (10 lessons)

Piano and violin from age 5. Ten lessons in the term.

€290

Children's piano or strings, 45 min weekly, per term

A longer weekly lesson across the same term.

€420

Adult beginners, 45 min weekly, per term

Adults of any age. One 45-minute lesson each week.

€450

Ear and theory group (max 6), per term

A small group, no more than six pupils.

€140

Friday evening ensemble, per term

Friday only. Other weekdays, the last lessons end at 21:30.

€120

Registration is €35 once per year. A sibling discount of 10 percent is applied in the office; it is not a separate price line.

Enrolment

How to begin

The trial is a single 30-minute meeting with a teacher and does not replace the registration fee.

  1. Book the free trial lesson.
  2. Meet a teacher for 30 minutes.
  3. Choose an instrument and a weekly slot.
  4. Start the term and pay the €35 registration.

Book a free trial

Changes

Changing or stopping lessons

To change or stop lessons, call the office Monday to Friday between 13:00 and 18:00 and speak with Sofie De Smet. The school does not publish a separate cancellation charge.

pages.title: FAQ
pages.content:
FAQ

Questions families ask

If you are unsure whether five is right for your child, the trial is the place to find out: book it, come to Lindenhof 14, and spend 30 minutes with a teacher before you choose a weekly slot.

From what age can a child start?

Piano and violin start at five. Adults may begin at any age, with no upper limit. Guitar, cello and voice are taught in the same building by Tomás Rivera, Jonas Weber and Amara Okonkwo. The school does not set a starting age for those three in its published fees, so the office will say whether a younger child can begin when you book.

What does a child's term cost?

Children's piano and strings are priced at 30 minutes weekly for €290 per term, ten lessons, or 45 minutes weekly for €420 per term. A trial lesson of 30 minutes is free.

How large are the lessons?

There are 240 pupils across the eight teachers. Lessons run in six teaching rooms, so a first lesson is not held in a large class.

How long is the teaching year?

The year is thirty teaching weeks, September to June. Lessons run Monday to Friday 14:00 to 21:30 and Saturday 09:00 to 18:00; the building is closed on Sunday.

What happens at the free trial?

The trial is a single 30-minute meeting with a teacher and does not replace the registration fee. To begin, book the free trial, meet a teacher for 30 minutes, choose an instrument and a weekly slot, then start the term and pay the €35 registration.

Can adults begin?

Yes. Adults may begin at any age. Adult beginners take a 45-minute weekly lesson at €450 per term, with lessons starting at 19:15.

Is there a sibling discount?

A sibling discount of 10 percent is applied in the office; it is not a separate price line.

How do I change or stop lessons?

To change or stop lessons, call the office Monday to Friday between 13:00 and 18:00 and speak with Sofie De Smet. The school does not publish a separate cancellation charge.

Are the recitals examinations?

They are not examinations, and the school does not attach a pass mark or a prize to them. There are two each year, in December and June, in the Long Room.

Where can I reach the office?

The office and telephone are open Monday to Friday 13:00 to 18:00, and Sofie De Smet answers them. There is no separate Sunday number.

Teaching hours are Monday to Friday 14:00 to 21:30 and Saturday 09:00 to 18:00. She is office staff, not one of the eight teachers.

Contact

Ask for a free trial lesson

Write or call during those office hours to book a free 30-minute trial lesson, to ask about a weekly slot, or to ask about seats for a recital. The contact form on this page is read by the office in those same hours. Fees, once you enrol, are the published EUR prices, plus registration of €35 once a year.

pages.title: Privacy
pages.content:
Privacy

What the office keeps

Neiro Music keeps the details you send when you enquire, book a trial, or enrol: your name, the pupil's name and age where you give it, a telephone number, an email address, the instrument, and the weekly slot you choose. Those details are used by the office at Lindenhof 14, 9000 Ghent, to arrange the free 30-minute trial, to take the yearly registration of €35, and to place a pupil with one of the eight teachers.

Sofie De Smet handles office messages Monday to Friday from 13:00 to 18:00. Messages sent through the contact form are read for the reply and are not used for a separate mailing list.

If you want a detail corrected or removed, write to the office during those hours and say which pupil the note concerns. The school teaches children from five and adults of any age, and a parent's contact is the one stored for a child.

posts.title: The June recital in the Long Room
posts.excerpt: Pupils play in the Long Room in June, the second of the two recitals in the teaching year.
posts.content:
The June recital is the second time in the year that Neiro Music asks pupils to play for anyone other than their teacher. The first is in December. Both evenings are held in the Long Room at Lindenhof 14, 9000 Ghent, the larger of the two floors in the converted print works. Sixty chairs face a low stage and a grand piano. Warm lamps do the lighting. The six teaching rooms stay as they are; the recital does not move lessons into a hired hall.

The room holds the school's ordinary scale. A pupil who has spent the week in a teaching room with one teacher walks a short corridor and plays for the families already known from the coat hooks in the entrance. There is no competition attached to the evening, no prize, and no outside jury. The recital is simply the evening when a pupil plays work from lessons once, in front of other people. When that playing is done, the term ends.

June closes a teaching year of thirty weeks that begins in September. Children's piano and strings at thirty minutes a week are billed as a term of ten lessons at €290. A forty-five minute weekly lesson is €420 per term. Adult beginners, also forty-five minutes weekly, are €450 per term. The ear and theory group, no more than six around the table, is €140 per term. None of those fees is a ticket to the recital. Families who want a seat ask the office.

Who plays depends on the lessons, not on a published ranking. In December, Noor, aged seven, played violin after a single term. That is the only first-recital account the school cites, and it is not offered as a pattern everyone will follow. A pupil who started later in the year may sit in the sixty seats and listen. Adult beginners are welcome on the same stage. Pieter, at fifty-eight, began piano as an adult and now plays duets with his granddaughter; an evening like June is where that kind of work can be heard without being turned into a showcase.

Strings have a clear path through the week before they reach the Long Room. At 16:45 the strings room is in use. Léa Fournier teaches violin. Jonas Weber teaches cello. The Haddad sisters, ten and thirteen, play piano and cello together in the Friday evening ensemble rather than only on recital day. That ensemble meets at 20:30 on Fridays, directed by Marco Bellini, and costs €120 per term. On the other weekdays the last lessons simply end at 21:30.

Piano pupils come from two hours. First lessons of the afternoon begin at 15:30, often a child at the start of study, from the age of five. Adult beginners are taught from 19:15 by Priya Raman. Ilse Marchetti, who founded the school in 2011 and still teaches piano, plays in the same building as her pupils; the recital is not a faculty concert. Voice with Amara Okonkwo and guitar with Tomás Rivera belong on the same evening when those pupils have something ready. Hannah Lindgren's ear and theory group does not perform as a class. The group remains a table of at most six, at 18:00, with manuscript paper and a metronome.

The office, run by Sofie De Smet, confirms the June date by telephone Monday to Friday from 13:00 to 18:00. Teaching itself runs later, Monday to Friday 14:00 to 21:30 and Saturday 09:00 to 18:00, and the building is closed on Sunday. A pupil who is not yet enrolled can still come to a recital as a listener and book the free trial afterwards: thirty minutes with a teacher, at no charge, then a choice of instrument and weekly slot, then the start of a term and the registration fee of €35 once in the year. A sibling discount of ten percent is arranged by the office when two children from the same family both take lessons. It does not change who may play in June.

If you are bringing a child, arrive by the entrance hall. Cases and coats stay on the hooks. The Long Room is the only room set with sixty chairs. Phones are best left quiet; the point of the hour is the same one the lessons chase all year, which is hearing a note clearly in a room that is otherwise still. When the last piece ends, the school returns to ordinary hours until September. The next gathering of this kind is the December recital, again in the Long Room, again without a prize list.
